slides.title: Riemannian Geometry: Intrinsic Measurement on Surfaces
slides.notes: Open the lecture by shifting attention from surfaces as subsets of space to surfaces as places where tangent vectors can be measured. The slide should make the metric ellipse the protagonist: it tells us which tangent directions count as unit length. Emphasize that the rest of the chapter is a chain of consequences from this local measurement rule.

slides.title: From Tangent Measurements to Global Invariants
slides.notes: Use this as a contract for the lecture. Students should know that the order is not arbitrary: a metric lets us measure, measurement selects the compatible connection, the connection defines geodesics and curvature, and curvature finally enters global theorems. The recurring question is whether an object is geometric or merely a coordinate record.

slides.title: Geometric Surfaces Carry Tangent Inner Products
slides.notes: Introduce the definition with the warning that coefficients are how the metric is written, not what the metric is. The visual separates the parameter domain from the surface and then places the metric ellipse directly in a tangent plane. Ask students which items would change under a different chart and which measurement statement would remain true.

slides.title: The First Fundamental Form Is a Measuring Device
slides.notes: This slide turns the first fundamental form into an operational object. The matrix is useful because it converts coordinate velocities into intrinsic speeds, and the ellipse gives students a picture of positive definiteness. Stress that a curve can wiggle in parameter space while its length is computed by the metric, not by the drawing of the parameter grid.

slides.title: Orthonormal Frames Make the Metric Look Standard
slides.notes: The frame is an instrument rather than an extra geometric object. At one point the metric looks like the Euclidean dot product, but the price is that the frame changes from point to point. This is where connection forms enter: they measure the rotation needed to compare nearby instruments.

slides.title: Covariant Derivative Keeps the Tangent Part
slides.notes: Make the projection idea very explicit. In Euclidean space we can differentiate a vector field normally, but the result may point partly away from the tangent plane. The covariant derivative is the surface's answer to differentiation because it discards the normal component and keeps the change that a surface-bound observer can detect.

slides.title: Parallel Transport Preserves Length but Can Rotate Direction
slides.notes: Parallel transport is the cleanest way to let students feel curvature without a formula first. The vector never changes according to the surface connection, yet a loop can bring it back rotated. This apparent paradox is productive: length preservation and direction preservation around closed paths are different claims on a curved surface.

slides.title: Geodesics Have Zero Intrinsic Acceleration
slides.notes: Use the contrast between the two curves to separate visual intuition from the definition. A geodesic on a drawn surface can look curved because the drawing is extrinsic, while the intrinsic acceleration condition is about tangent projection. The warning prevents the common overstatement that geodesics are always shortest over arbitrary distances.

slides.title: Curvature Is Frame Rotation Per Unit Area
slides.notes: This slide connects the transport picture to the curvature formula. The small loop is not meant to prove the structure equation, but it gives the right mental model: curvature is the density of rotational mismatch produced by parallel transport. Point out that in two dimensions the curvature form collapses to one scalar times the area form.

slides.title: Three Constant-Curvature Behaviors
slides.notes: The three panels should be read as behavior diagrams, not as literal exhaustive models. Positive curvature encourages geodesics to meet, zero curvature preserves the Euclidean comparison, and negative curvature pushes initially nearby geodesics apart. This prepares the audience for Gauss-Bonnet, where the sign of curvature influences angle accounting.

slides.title: Clairaut Coordinates Reveal a Conserved Quantity
slides.notes: Present Clairaut's relation as a conservation law rather than as an isolated trick. Rotational symmetry gives a direction that the metric does not distinguish, and that symmetry produces a constant along geodesics. Have students inspect the surface of revolution: as the radius changes, the angle term must compensate if the curve remains geodesic.

slides.title: Gauss-Bonnet Balances Curvature and Turning
slides.notes: This is the bridge from curvature as a local density to curvature as a global accounting term. The formula has three visible ingredients: interior curvature, boundary turning, and corner turning. Point out that no single term is automatically topological, but the sum is forced to match the Euler characteristic of the region.

slides.title: Total Curvature Knows the Euler Characteristic
slides.notes: The closed-surface formula deserves a pause because it is one of the chapter's conceptual peaks. The integrand can vary dramatically across a chosen metric, yet the total is locked to the Euler characteristic. Use the three icons to emphasize that adding handles changes the allowable total curvature by a fixed topological amount.

slides.title: Vector-Field Index Counts Forced Singularities
slides.notes: Connect vector-field index to the same accounting habit as Gauss-Bonnet. Around a zero, the field directions rotate, and the winding number records that local behavior. The striking point is global: on some surfaces zeros cannot be eliminated because the total index must match the Euler characteristic.

slides.title: What Chapter 07 Adds to the Geometry Toolkit
slides.notes: Close by restoring the full chain from the opening slide. The chapter is not a bag of formulas; it is a sequence of increasingly global consequences of tangent-plane measurement. The final sentence to leave with students is that Riemannian geometry begins locally, but its most powerful theorems explain what the local data must add up to globally.
